pos: n. / adj. (speaking against a man behind his back; the tongue that wounds the absent)
etymology: English back + bite — to bite a man where he cannot see the teeth. The AV uses it for Hebrew ragal, to foot it, to go about from house to house carrying a report, and for Greek katalalia, a speaking-down.
biblical_def:
Solomon puts it in a proverb of weather: The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue. The picture is a face that will not receive the report — a countenance so plainly displeased that the talebearer folds his errand and goes elsewhere. That is the proverb's cure, and it is worth noticing how ordinary it is. Scripture does not ask the hearer to argue the slanderer down or to convene a hearing; it asks him to look unwilling. The backbiter needs a listener the way fire needs wood, and the withdrawal of the face is the withdrawal of the fuel.

The sin is defined by the absence of the man spoken against. A charge brought to his face is a rebuke, and rebuke is commanded; the same words carried behind him are backbiting, because he cannot answer them, and the hearer receives one side of a matter as though it were the whole. David marks the citizen of God's hill by the negative: He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour. Three clauses, and the last is the sharpest — a man may originate no reproach and still be guilty of taking one up, of lending his ear and then his mouth to a story he did not start. Paul lists backbiters among the marks of a mind God has given over (Romans 1:30), and warns the Corinthians that he fears to find backbitings and whisperings in a church that thought its trouble was doctrinal.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to censure, slander or speak reproachfully of the absent.
webster_full: BACKBITE, v.t. To censure, slander, reproach, or speak evil of the absent.
BACKBITER, n. One who slanders, calumniates or speaks ill of the absent.
SLANDER, n. A false tale or report maliciously uttered, and tending to injure the reputation of another.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt or derision; contumelious or opprobrious language.
TALEBEARER, n. A person who officiously tells tales; one who impertinently communicates intelligence or anecdotes, and makes mischief in society.
scriptures: Proverbs 25:23
The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue.
Psalm 15:3
He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour.
Romans 1:30
Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,
2 Corinthians 12:20

For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults:
corruption_summary: Backbiting survives in the church under better names — a prayer request that carries the facts, a word of concern, a private processing of a brother's fault with someone who has no business in it.
corruption_paragraphs: No one in a Reformed congregation announces that he is about to backbite. The report arrives dressed: I only tell you so you can pray, or I need to process this with someone, or the still safer I am not saying anything I would not say to his face — which, if it were true, would have been said to his face. Each of these keeps the substance of Psalm 15:3 and changes the label. The test Scripture gives is not the tone of the telling but the absence of the man told about and the errand of the telling: does the hearer need this to help, or only to know? Matthew 18 gives the sequence — go to him alone first — and every step of it is designed to keep a fault from becoming a story.

The second corruption is subtler and touches the listener. Modern speech has made a virtue of hearing everyone out, so declining a report feels like a failure of sympathy. Solomon assumes the opposite: the man of God is expected to be visibly unwilling, and his unwillingness is a mercy to the absent. Refusing to take up a reproach is not coldness toward the speaker; it is faithfulness to the one who cannot defend himself. Where no wood is, the fire goes out, and the hearer who will not burn is doing more for peace than the peacemaker who listens to both sides of a matter only one side knows is being tried.
roots_summary: Hebrew ragal (H7270), to go about on foot as a slanderer; Greek katalalia (G2636), a speaking-against; katalalos (G2637), a backbiter.
roots_lines: Hebrew ragal (H7270) — literally to foot it; the same root gives the spy, and the backbiter is a man who goes about gathering and carrying.
Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach; the thing Psalm 15 forbids a man even to take up once another has dropped it.
Greek katalalia (G2636) — a speaking-down; the noun Paul feared to find at Corinth and Peter commands the newborn to lay aside.
Greek katalalos (G2637) — a backbiter; one of the marks in Romans 1 of a mind given over to a reprobate state.
Greek psithurismos (G5587) — whispering; backbiting's quieter twin, standing beside it in the Corinthian list.
usage: “so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue” — the unwilling face as the appointed cure.
“He that backbiteth not with his tongue” — a mark of the man who shall abide in God's tabernacle.
“nor taketh up a reproach” — the hearer is guilty too.

pos: n. pl. (those who circulate false or damaging report; in 1 Timothy 3:11, the Greek word is devils)
etymology: From Old French esclandre, a scandal, itself from Latin scandalum, a stumbling-block. In the AV it renders Hebrew dibbah, an evil report, and Greek diabolos — the word elsewhere translated devil.
biblical_def:
Paul is listing the qualifications of those who serve the church, and when he comes to the women he writes: Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. The word behind slanderers is diabolos. It is the word the New Testament uses more than thirty times for Satan himself, and Paul spends it here, without apology, on a woman who carries reports. That is the measure Scripture takes of the sin. The accuser of the brethren has an occupation, and anyone in the congregation who takes up the same trade is doing his work in his voice.

The Psalms know the sin from underneath, from the position of the man it falls on. Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off — and the adverb is the whole of it, privily, in secret, where the charge cannot be answered. David pairs it at once with the high look and the proud heart, because slander is a species of self-exaltation: a man raises his own standing by lowering another's, and does it cheaply, at no risk, in a room the accused will never enter. Solomon adds the cold verdict that closes the matter: he that uttereth a slander, is a fool. Not merely unkind — a fool, in the Proverbs sense, a man at odds with the fear of the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): those who utter a false tale or report, maliciously, to injure another's reputation.
webster_full: SLANDERER, n. One who slanders; a defamer; a calumniator.
SLANDER, n. A false tale or report maliciously uttered, and tending to injure the reputation of another by lessening him in the esteem of his fellow citizens.
CALUMNY, n. Slander; false accusation of a crime or offense, knowingly or maliciously made or reported, to the injury of another.
DEFAME, v.t. To slander; falsely and maliciously to utter words respecting another which tend to injure his reputation.
GRAVE, a. Of weighty character; serious; sober; solemn; not light, trifling or jocose.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 3:11
Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things.
Psalm 101:5
Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer.
Proverbs 10:18
He that hideth hatred with lying lips, and he that uttereth a slander, is a fool.
Psalm 50:20
Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother; thou slanderest thine own mother's son.
corruption_summary: Slander is renamed accountability, transparency, or speaking truth to power, and the renaming does nothing whatever to the ninth commandment.
corruption_paragraphs: The public trade in reputation now runs faster than any court and answers to no one. A charge posted before it is proved is read by thousands, the retraction by a handful, and the man is tried in a room he was never summoned to. The vocabulary that carries this is borrowed from virtue — accountability, transparency, exposure, holding to account — and some of what it carries is true, which is precisely what makes the rest of it dangerous. Scripture does not forbid the bringing of charges. It forbids bringing them privily, and it sets a fence around the process: at the mouth of two or three witnesses, before the elders, against an elder receive not an accusation otherwise (1 Timothy 5:19). Where the fence is down, the diabolos is at work whatever the platform calls him.

Inside the church the same sin keeps quieter hours. Paul thought it worth naming in the very paragraph on who may serve, which tells us he expected to find it there. A congregation can hold sound doctrine, sing the psalms, and still be eaten out by report — and no confession ever written protects a church from the tongue by itself. What protects it is the ordinary discipline of Matthew 18, the refusal to hear a charge that has not first been brought to the man, and the humility to remember that the accuser of the brethren works nights and does not need a title.
roots_summary: Hebrew dibbah (H1681), an evil report; ragal (H7270), to slander; Greek diabolos (G1228), an accuser — the New Testament's word for the devil.
roots_lines: Greek diabolos (G1228) — an accuser, a slanderer; used of Satan throughout the New Testament, and of church members in 1 Timothy 3:11, 2 Timothy 3:3 and Titus 2:3.
Hebrew dibbah (H1681) — an evil report; the word for the slander the ten spies brought up on the land.
Hebrew ragal (H7270) — to go about as a talebearer; the verb behind slandereth in Psalm 15:3.
Hebrew lashon (H3956) — tongue; the member James calls a world of iniquity.
Greek blasphemia (G988) — railing, evil speaking; slander aimed upward becomes blasphemy.
usage: “not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things” — a qualification, because the sin is found in churches.
“Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off” — the secrecy is the offence.
“he that uttereth a slander, is a fool” — Proverbs' final word on the trade.

pos: adv. (by way of slander; in the manner of a false report knowingly circulated)
etymology: The adverb of slander, from Old French esclandre and Latin scandalum, a stumbling-block. It appears once in the Authorized Version, in Paul's parenthesis at Romans 3:8.
biblical_def:
The word occurs once, and it is the apostle speaking about himself: And not rather, (as we be slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say,) Let us do evil, that good may come? whose damnation is just. Paul has been preaching justification by grace apart from works, and his enemies have drawn the obvious caricature — if grace abounds where sin abounds, then sin freely. He puts the charge in parentheses, which is itself instructive: he does not build the chapter around his own defence. He names the misreport, states its source (some affirm that we say), pronounces the judgment of those who spread it, and returns to the argument.

Two things in that verse govern how a believer bears a false report. The first is that Paul does not deny being slandered, and does not pretend it does not sting; he says plainly that the thing said of him was said. The second is that he leaves the damnation of the slanderers with God in a single clause and does not litigate it further. The Lord Himself was accused of gluttony and winebibbing, of casting out devils by Beelzebub, of destroying the temple; the servant is not above his master. Peter's counsel to a church under the same weather is not to answer every charge but to live so that the charge dies of embarrassment: that, whereas they speak evil of you, as of evildoers, they may be ashamed that falsely accuse your good conversation in Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): with slander; with false and malicious report; calumniously.
webster_full: SLANDEROUSLY, adv. With slander; with false and malicious reproach.
SLANDEROUS, a. Uttering defamatory words; containing slander.
CALUMNIOUSLY, adv. In a slanderous manner; falsely and maliciously.
REPORT, n. An account returned; a statement or relation of facts given in reply to inquiry, or by a person authorized to examine.
FALSELY, adv. In a manner contrary to truth and justice; erroneously.
scriptures: Romans 3:8
And not rather, (as we be slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say,) Let us do evil, that good may come? whose damnation is just.
1 Peter 3:16
Having a good conscience; that, whereas they speak evil of you, as of evildoers, they may be ashamed that falsely accuse your good conversation in Christ.
Matthew 5:11
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
Psalm 31:13
For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life.
corruption_summary: The gospel of free grace has always been slanderously reported as a license to sin, and the misreport is answered by Romans 6, not by trimming the doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 3:8 records the oldest standing slander against the Reformed doctrine of justification: that grace apart from works must mean sin without consequence. It was brought against Paul in the first century and against Luther in the sixteenth, and the reappearance of the charge in every generation is one of the quiet evidences that the doctrine being preached is Paul's. The answer Scripture gives is not a retreat into some measured middle where faith is mostly free. It is Romans 6 — shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid — the argument that union with Christ in His death makes continuance in sin a contradiction in terms, not merely a bad idea. A doctrine that could never be slandered this way would not be the doctrine Paul was slandered for.

The second temptation runs the other direction: to answer the misreport by preaching a gospel so hedged with conditions that no one could possibly mistake it for freedom. That is how the free offer gets buried under qualifications, and how a congregation ends up unable to say plainly that salvation is by grace alone through faith alone. Paul did not do it. He put the slander in a parenthesis, left the judgment with God, and went on to write the eighth chapter. Bearing a false report without amending the truth to escape it is part of what it costs to preach the whole counsel of God.
roots_summary: Greek blasphemeo (G987), to speak injuriously, to defame; the passive here rendered slanderously reported.
roots_lines: Greek blasphemeo (G987) — to revile, to speak injuriously; rendered slanderously reported at Romans 3:8.
Greek phemi (G5346) — to affirm, to say; the verb behind as some affirm that we say.
Greek krima (G2917) — judgment, condemnation; whose damnation is just.
Hebrew dibbah (H1681) — the evil report David hears round about him in Psalm 31:13.
Greek epereazo (G1908) — to accuse falsely, to insult; Peter's word for those who falsely accuse a good conversation.
usage: “as we be slanderously reported” — the apostle names the caricature of his own gospel.
“whose damnation is just” — judgment left with God in one clause.
“say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” — the Lord counts it blessedness.

pos: n. pl. (secret talk against another; the quiet circulation of a damaging report)
etymology: From Old English hwisprian, to speak under the breath — an imitative word. It renders Greek psithurismos, from psithuros, a whisperer, a word the Greeks used of the hiss of a snake and of the murmur of an enchanter's spell.
biblical_def:
Paul is bracing himself for what he may find at Corinth: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults. Eight words, and they run from the loudest to the quietest and back to the loudest again. Whisperings sit in the middle of the list because that is where they sit in the life of a congregation — below the noise, under the surface, doing the work that produces the tumults at the end. Nothing in the list is doctrinal error. This is a church in good standing on paper being pulled apart by how its members talk.

The Greek word is psithurismos, and it carries the sound with it: a hiss, a murmur, the noise of an enchantment. Classical Greek used the cognate for the whispering of a spell, and Solomon had already caught the effect exactly — a whisperer separateth chief friends. Not enemies; chief friends. The whisper does not work by argument. It works by dropping a half-sentence into a friendship and letting it swell there, and the man who dropped it is three rooms away by the time it does its work. Paul has the noun again in Romans 1:29, where whisperers stands in the catalogue of a mind given over, between deceit and backbiting. Scripture never treats the quietness of the sin as an extenuation of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): speaking in a low voice; in the plural, secret and malicious talk; the private circulation of reports.
webster_full: WHISPERING, ppr. Speaking in a low voice; speaking in private; telling secretly.
WHISPERER, n. One who whispers; a tattler; one who tells secrets; a conveyer of intelligence secretly.
WHISPER, v.i. To speak with a low, hissing or sibilant voice; to speak with suspicion or timorous caution.
TUMULT, n. The commotion, disturbance or agitation of a multitude, usually accompanied with great noise, uproar and confusion of voices.
STRIFE, n. Exertion or contention for superiority; contest of emulation, either by intellectual or physical efforts.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 12:20

For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults:
Romans 1:29
Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers,
Proverbs 16:28
A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends.
Proverbs 26:20
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
corruption_summary: Whispering is not a small sin quietly committed; Paul files it between backbiting and tumult because the tumult is what it is for.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern church rarely disciplines a whisper. It will discipline a public scandal, and it will labour over doctrinal deviation, but the slow hissing that empties a congregation is left alone because no single sentence of it is actionable. Every fragment is deniable — a look, a pause, an I probably should not say — and the man who assembles them into a campaign can honestly say he never made an accusation. Scripture does not grade the sin by how much of it fits in one sentence. Paul names whisperings as a thing a church can be found in, alongside wraths and tumults, and the pastoral point of 2 Corinthians 12:20 is that he expects to find them together, because the one produces the others.

There is no significant progressive redefinition of this word to rebut; the corruption is practical, and it lives in congregations that would call themselves confessional. The principle to recover is Solomon's fuel rule. Whispering requires two mouths and at least one ear, and the ear is the part most easily withdrawn. Where no wood is, the fire goes out — which means the hearer who declines the half-sentence, and says so plainly, has done more for the peace of the church than a dozen meetings will do afterward.
roots_summary: Greek psithurismos (G5587), a whispering; psithuristes (G5588), a whisperer; Hebrew nirgan (H5372), a talebearer or murmurer.
roots_lines: Greek psithurismos (G5587) — a whispering, a hiss; used once, in Paul's list of what he feared to find at Corinth.
Greek psithuristes (G5588) — a whisperer; in the Romans 1 catalogue of a reprobate mind.
Hebrew nirgan (H5372) — a whisperer, a talebearer; the man of Proverbs 16:28 who separates chief friends.
Hebrew lachash (H3908) — a whisper, a charm, an incantation; the same sound used of a serpent-charmer.
Greek akatastasia (G181) — tumult, disorder; the last word in Paul's list and the end of the road that whispering builds.
usage: “backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults” — the order is a diagnosis.
“a whisperer separateth chief friends” — the target is friendship, not enmity.
“where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth” — the cure is the withheld ear.

pos: n. pl. (those who complain against God under their breath; grumblers at His providence)
etymology: From Latin murmur, a low continuous sound — an imitative word for the noise of a crowd or a stream. In the AV it renders Hebrew lun, to lodge as a complaint, and Greek goggustes, itself an imitation of the sound.
biblical_def:
Jude is describing the men who have crept in unawares, and when he comes to characterize them he begins with the mouth: These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaketh great swelling words. The order of that sentence is worth sitting with. Murmuring comes first, walking after lusts second, great swelling words last — the small discontented noise is named as the front edge of the whole apostasy, and the loud boasting is where it ends up. The wilderness generation is Jude's standing example throughout the epistle, and the wilderness is where the word was learned.

Israel murmured at Marah for water, at the Red Sea for fear, at Kadesh for the land. Moses answered every time with the same correction, and it is the doctrinal heart of the word: your murmurings are not against us, but against the LORD. A murmur is always aimed higher than the man it is spoken to. The complaint about the food is a complaint about the One who sends it; the complaint about the leader is a complaint about the One who set him there. That is why the punishment fell so heavily — Paul reminds Corinth that they murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer — and why the apostolic command is so total: Do all things without murmurings and disputings. All things. There is no category of providence exempted, and no volume quiet enough to make the murmur something other than what it is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): those who utter complaints in a low voice; grumblers; repiners at what befalls them.
webster_full: MURMURER, n. One who murmurs; one who complains unreasonably; a repiner.
MURMUR, v.i. To grumble; to complain; to utter complaints in a low, half articulated voice.
COMPLAINER, n. One who complains, or expresses grief; one who laments; a murmurer.
REPINE, v.i. To fret one's self; to be discontented; to feel inward discontent which preys on the spirits.
DISPUTING, ppr. Contending by words or arguments; controverting; calling in question.
scriptures: Jude 1:16
These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaketh great swelling words, having men's persons in admiration because of advantage.
Exodus 16:8

And Moses said, This shall be, when the LORD shall give you in the evening flesh to eat, and in the morning bread to the full; for that the LORD heareth your murmurings which ye murmur against him: and what are we? your murmurings are not against us, but against the LORD.
1 Corinthians 10:10
Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer.
Philippians 2:14
Do all things without murmurings and disputings:
corruption_summary: Discontent is treated as honest emotional expression rather than as speech against providence, and the wilderness is emptied of its warning.
corruption_paragraphs: The strongest pressure on this word today is the counsel to get it all out — to name every grievance, to refuse to suppress, to treat the unedited complaint as a form of honesty. Scripture is not against lament. The Psalms complain to God at length and in detail, and the book of Job is a long, loud, unedited protest that God Himself vindicates over against the men who tried to tidy it. The line Scripture draws is not between speaking and silence but between complaining to God and murmuring about Him — between Psalm 88, which addresses Him through eighteen verses of darkness, and Numbers 14, which talks about Him to the neighbours. Lament is faith speaking in the dark. Murmuring is unbelief speaking behind His back.

The second loss is the wilderness itself. Paul says plainly that those things were written for our admonition, and 1 Corinthians 10 is an apostle handling that history as history — real bread, real water, real graves. A reading that files the murmuring narratives as folklore takes the warning out with the facts. What is left to recover is Moses' sentence, which is the whole doctrine in eleven words: your murmurings are not against us, but against the LORD. Every believer tempted to grumble about a providence, a leader, or a portion has that verse standing across the road.
roots_summary: Hebrew lun (H3885), to murmur or lodge a complaint; Greek goggustes (G1113), a grumbler; goggusmos (G1112), a murmuring.
roots_lines: Greek goggustes (G1113) — a grumbler; used once, of the men Jude describes as crept in unawares.
Greek goggusmos (G1112) — a murmuring; the noun Paul forbids at Philippians 2:14.
Hebrew lun (H3885) — to lodge, and so to lodge a complaint; the wilderness word from Exodus to Numbers.
Greek mempsimoiros (G3202) — a complainer, one discontented with his lot; Jude's second word, standing beside the first.
Greek olothreutes (G3644) — the destroyer; the agent by whom the murmurers of 1 Corinthians 10:10 fell.
usage: “These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts” — the small noise at the head of the list.
“your murmurings are not against us, but against the LORD” — the doctrine in a sentence.
“Do all things without murmurings and disputings” — no providence exempted.

pos: n. pl. (those who swear falsely; in Malachi 3:5, men who take the LORD's name to a lie)
etymology: From Old English swerian, to take an oath. In the Authorized Version false swearers renders a Hebrew participle from shaba, to swear, joined to sheqer, falsehood — men who swear a lie.
biblical_def:
Malachi has been answering a generation that asked where the God of judgment is, and the answer comes as a list of the first men He will meet when He arrives: I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless. The false swearer stands in company — sorcery, adultery, wage-theft, the crushing of the widow. He is not a lesser offender who slipped into a serious list. To swear falsely is to call God as a witness to a lie, which is to attempt to make Him a party to it, and Scripture ranks it where that attempt deserves.

The third commandment governs the whole matter, and Zechariah sees the curse for it going out over the face of the whole earth on a flying roll, one side for the thief and the other for him that sweareth. Our Lord tightens the fence rather than loosening it. He does not abolish the lawful oath — He answered one Himself under adjuration, and Paul calls God for a record upon his soul — but He forbids the whole apparatus of graded swearing by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem, by the head, by which men manufactured oaths they did not intend to keep. Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay. A man whose plain word is good has no use for an oath ladder, and a man who needs one has already told us something.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): those who swear; in the bad sense, men who take an oath falsely or profanely.
webster_full: SWEARER, n. One who swears; one who calls God to witness for the truth of his declaration.
SWEAR, v.i. To affirm or utter a solemn declaration, with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
PERJURY, n. The act or crime of wilfully making a false oath, when lawfully administered.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
PROFANE, a. Irreverent to sacred things; irreverent to God or to holy things.
scriptures: Malachi 3:5

And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and that turn aside the stranger from his right, and fear not me, saith the LORD of hosts.
Zechariah 5:3

Then said he unto me, This is the curse that goeth forth over the face of the whole earth: for every one that stealeth shall be cut off as on this side according to it; and every one that sweareth shall be cut off as on that side according to it.
Matthew 5:34
But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne:
James 5:12
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.
corruption_summary: Profanity is treated as mere coarseness of speech, and the third commandment is reduced to a rule about vocabulary rather than about the truth of what a man says under God's name.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet over this word. The first shrinks the third commandment to a list of forbidden syllables, so that a man who never says the word may swear a hundred false things and think himself clear. Malachi's false swearer is not a man with a coarse mouth; he is a man whose word cannot be trusted and who has dressed the untrustworthy word in God's name to get it believed. The second error runs the other way and reads our Lord's Swear not at all as abolishing the civil and ecclesiastical oath altogether — a reading the confession rejects, since Scripture records God swearing by Himself, Paul calling God to record, and the Lord answering when adjured by the high priest.

The 1689 Confession states the balance plainly: a lawful oath is a part of religious worship, wherein the person swearing in truth calls God to witness what he asserts, and it may be taken when imposed by lawful authority. What is forbidden is the vain oath, the false oath, and the whole trade in graded swearing our Lord names — by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem, by the head — which existed for one purpose, to sound binding while leaving an exit. The principle to recover is that a Christian's bare yes should carry the weight other men need an oath to borrow.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaba (H7650), to swear, literally to seven oneself; sheqer (H8267), falsehood; Greek omnuo (G3660), to swear.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaba (H7650) — to swear; the root is seven, from the sevenfold witness by which oaths were bound.
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, a lie; joined to the participle it gives Malachi's false swearers.
Greek omnuo (G3660) — to swear, to take an oath; the verb our Lord restrains in Matthew 5 and James repeats.
Greek horkos (G3727) — an oath; that which is sworn, and in James the thing not to be multiplied.
Greek epiorkeo (G1964) — to forswear, to swear falsely; the sin Malachi's swift witness meets first.
usage: “a swift witness against... false swearers” — named beside sorcery and adultery.
“every one that sweareth shall be cut off” — the flying roll, one side for each.
“let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay” — the Christian's bare word as the oath.

pos: n. / ppr. (the circulating of an evil report; the destruction of a man's name behind him)
etymology: From Latin diffamare, to spread abroad a report, from fama, rumour or reputation. In Jeremiah 20:10 it renders Hebrew dibbah, an evil report or slander — the same word used of the report the ten spies brought up on the land.
biblical_def:
Jeremiah has just been put in the stocks by Pashur the priest, and the lament that follows is the rawest passage in the book: For I heard the defaming of many, fear on every side. Report, say they, and we will report it. All my familiars watched for my halting. The phrase fear on every side is the name Jeremiah had himself given to Pashur, thrown back at him now as a taunt. What breaks the prophet is not the stocks but the source of the whispering — all my familiars, the men of his own circle, watching not for his welfare but for his stumble, waiting with a report already half-written.

Paul knows the same weather from the apostolic side: Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day. The response in that verse is one word long and it is the whole Christian answer — we intreat, we entreat, we plead kindly. Not we retaliate, not we withdraw. And Jeremiah, in the very next breath after his complaint, turns and says the thing that holds a man up under it: But the LORD is with me as a mighty terrible one: therefore my persecutors shall stumble, and they shall not prevail. The defaming is real, the fear is real, and the one sentence that answers both is that the LORD is with him. Scripture does not promise the prophet a cleared name in his lifetime. It promises him the presence of God while the name is being taken.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): slandering; speaking evil of; injuring the reputation by false report.
webster_full: DEFAME, v.t. To slander; falsely and maliciously to utter words respecting another which tend to injure his reputation or occupation.
DEFAMING, ppr. Slandering; injuring the good name and reputation.
DEFAMATION, n. The uttering of slanderous words with a view to injure another's reputation.
FAME, n. Public report or rumor; that which is said or reported abroad of a person.
OFFSCOURING, n. That which is scoured off; hence, refuse; recrement; any thing vile or despised.
scriptures: Jeremiah 20:10

For I heard the defaming of many, fear on every side. Report, say they, and we will report it. All my familiars watched for my halting, saying, Peradventure he will be enticed, and we shall prevail against him, and we shall take our revenge on him.
Jeremiah 20:11

But the LORD is with me as a mighty terrible one: therefore my persecutors shall stumble, and they shall not prevail: they shall be greatly ashamed; for they shall not prosper: their everlasting confusion shall never be forgotten.
1 Corinthians 4:13
Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day.
Psalm 31:13
For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life.
corruption_summary: Reputation is now destroyed at the speed of a network and restored at the speed of a court, and the gap between the two is where a great deal of modern cruelty lives.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah's familiars needed a city gate and a few days. The machinery has changed and the sin has not: a report goes out, is repeated by men who have not checked it because repeating is cheap, and by the time anything is established the man is already what the report said he was. Report, say they, and we will report it is a perfect description of a feed. What Scripture supplies against it is not a technique but a standing: the LORD is with him as a mighty terrible one. That is the sentence Jeremiah reaches for in the same paragraph as his complaint, and it is the only thing that holds when a name cannot be cleared.

For the one tempted to join the reporting, the fence is older than any platform. Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness (Exodus 23:1) forbids not only the raising of the report but the lending of a hand to one already raised — and a forward, a repetition, a nod is a hand. The ninth commandment binds the repeater as it binds the originator, and Paul's one-word answer under defamation, we intreat, remains the pattern for a believer whose name is being taken: entreat, keep a good conscience, and leave the vindication with God, who forgets nothing.
roots_summary: Hebrew dibbah (H1681), an evil report or whispering; Greek dusphemeo (G1425), to speak ill of, rendered defamed.
roots_lines: Hebrew dibbah (H1681) — an evil report; the same noun used of the slander the spies brought up upon the land.
Greek dusphemeo (G1425) — to speak injuriously; used once, of the apostles in 1 Corinthians 4:13.
Hebrew magor missabib (H4036) — fear on every side; the name Jeremiah gave Pashur, returned to him as a taunt.
Hebrew tsela (H6761) — a halting, a limp; what the familiars watched for.
Greek parakaleo (G3870) — to entreat, to plead kindly; Paul's whole answer to being defamed.
usage: “I heard the defaming of many, fear on every side” — the prophet in the stocks.
“Report, say they, and we will report it” — the machinery, unchanged.
“Being defamed, we intreat” — the apostolic answer in two words.

pos: n. pl. (in 1 Peter 2:1, evil speakings — the utterances by which a brother is torn down)
etymology: The plural of the verbal noun from Old English sprecan, to speak. Peter's phrase evil speakings renders Greek katalalia, a speaking-down, the same noun Paul uses for backbitings at Corinth.
biblical_def:
Peter has just told his readers that they are born again of incorruptible seed, and the first practical command that follows is a stripping: Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings. Five things, and the last is the mouth. The metaphor in laying aside is a garment taken off — the same word used of the witnesses laying down their clothes at Stephen's stoning — and the sentence does not end there. It runs on into the next verse: as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word. The clothes come off so that the appetite can come on. A believer who will not put away evil speaking will not grow, because the two occupy the same hours.

Note the company Peter keeps for the word. Malice is the disposition; guile is the crookedness; hypocrisy is the mask; envy is the engine; evil speaking is the exhaust. They are one machine, and the tongue is where it vents. That is why Paul, giving the same command to Ephesus, puts evil speaking at the end of a list that begins with bitterness — Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice — and why James makes the prohibition a matter of the law itself: Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother... speaketh evil of the law. The man who tears down a brother has appointed himself judge, and in doing so has stepped over the one Lawgiver who is able to save and to destroy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): utterances; in Peter's phrase, evil speakings — slanderous or reproachful words spoken of another.
webster_full: SPEAKING, n. The act of uttering words; discourse; the act of expressing thought by words.
EVIL-SPEAKING, n. Slander; defamation; censoriousness.
MALICE, n. Extreme enmity of heart, or malevolence; a disposition to injure others without cause.
GUILE, n. Craft; cunning; artifice; duplicity; deceit; usually in a bad sense.
HYPOCRISY, n. Simulation; a feigning to be what one is not; dissimulation in regard to moral or religious character.
scriptures: 1 Peter 2:1
Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings,
Ephesians 4:31
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:
James 4:11

Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law: but if thou judge the law, thou art not a doer of the law, but a judge.
Colossians 3:8
But now ye also put off all these; anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth.
corruption_summary: Evil speaking is defended as candour, and the honesty of a remark is offered as though it settled whether the remark should have been made.
corruption_paragraphs: The standing defence of evil speaking in our day is that it is true. I am only being honest is felt to end the argument, as though the ninth commandment forbade falsehood alone. It does not. James forbids speaking evil of a brother without any qualifier about accuracy, and Paul's corrupt communication is measured not by its truthfulness but by whether it edifies: that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers. A true word spoken to pull a man down is evil speaking; a true word spoken to build him up is a duty. The test is not the fact but the errand.

The second corruption is the assumption that the tongue is a small matter compared with doctrine or conduct. Peter puts evil speaking in a list of five things that must come off before a newborn believer can feed, and James devotes a chapter to the member no man can tame. The principle to recover is that the mouth is where sanctification is either demonstrated or exposed. A congregation may recite the confession and still be a place where reputations are spent freely, and Peter's order is exact: lay aside first, then desire the milk — the clothes come off before the growth comes on.
roots_summary: Greek katalalia (G2636), a speaking-against; apotithemi (G659), to lay aside as a garment; blasphemia (G988), railing or evil speaking.
roots_lines: Greek katalalia (G2636) — a speaking-down, evil speaking; Peter's word here and Paul's at 2 Corinthians 12:20.
Greek apotithemi (G659) — to put off, to lay aside as clothing; the verb governing all five items in 1 Peter 2:1.
Greek blasphemia (G988) — railing, evil speaking; Paul's term in the parallel command at Ephesians 4:31.
Greek sapros (G4550) — rotten, corrupt; the adjective on the communication forbidden at Ephesians 4:29.
Greek oikodome (G3619) — edifying, building up; the positive standard against which any word is measured.
usage: “laying aside all malice... and all evil speakings” — a garment taken off.
“He that speaketh evil of his brother... speaketh evil of the law” — the judge who outranks the Lawgiver.
“that which is good to the use of edifying” — the errand, not the accuracy, is the test.

pos: n. pl. (the covenant curses read aloud at Ebal; the sanctions of the broken law)
etymology: From Old English cursian, to curse. In Joshua 8:34 it renders Hebrew qelalah, a curse or execration, the formal counterpart to berakah, blessing — the two halves of the covenant sanction.
biblical_def:
Israel is standing in the pass between two mountains, and Joshua does exactly what Moses commanded: And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessings and cursings, according to all that is written in the book of the law. Half the tribes stood over against Gerizim and half over against Ebal, the ark and the priests between them, the stranger standing with the native-born; and the whole law was read aloud — not summarized, not sampled. The plural is the point. These are not spontaneous imprecations but the fixed sanctions of a covenant, published in advance so that no one could later say he had not been told the terms.

Deuteronomy 27 ends the recital with a sentence that reaches further than Israel: Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them. And all the people shall say, Amen. All the words — and the people were made to pronounce their own Amen over it. Paul takes that verse up in Galatians and shows what it does to every man who seeks life by obedience: as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse. Not may come under it; are under it. The cursings of Ebal are the law's honest statement of what it can do for a sinner, and they stand there until Christ, made a curse for us, hanging on a tree, takes them off the elect and leaves the blessing of Abraham in their place. Balaam's hired curse turned into a blessing at Beth-peor is the picture; Calvary is the substance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): imprecations of evil; in Scripture, the denunciations of divine wrath attached to the breach of the covenant.
webster_full: CURSING, n. Execration; the uttering of a curse; a dooming to evil.
CURSE, n. Malediction; the expression of a wish of evil to another; the denunciation of evil pronounced by God.
MALEDICTION, n. A curse or execration; a cursing; a denouncing of evil.
BLESSING, n. A prayer or solicitation imploring happiness upon another; the act of pronouncing good upon.
COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing.
scriptures: Joshua 8:34
And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessings and cursings, according to all that is written in the book of the law.
Deuteronomy 27:26
Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them. And all the people shall say, Amen.
Galatians 3:10
For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them.
Nehemiah 13:2
Because they met not the children of Israel with bread and with water, but hired Balaam against them, that he should curse them: howbeit our God turned the curse into a blessing.
corruption_summary: The covenant curses are read as primitive tribal religion rather than as the law's honest verdict, and with them goes the necessity of the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: A reading now common treats Ebal as the residue of an older and harsher stage of Israelite religion, outgrown by the prophets and abolished by Jesus. That is not how the New Testament handles it. Paul quotes Deuteronomy 27:26 as a live word with present force — as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse — and builds the doctrine of justification on the fact that the curse is real, is deserved, and must land somewhere. Soften the cursings and the cross becomes an excess: if the law never truly cursed, Christ was never truly made a curse for us, and Galatians 3:13 is left describing a rescue from nothing.

The second corruption is quieter and lives inside evangelical churches. The law is preached as advice, its sanctions omitted as unhelpful, and the result is a congregation that cannot account for why the Son of God had to die. Israel was made to say Amen to its own condemnation before it was given the land. That is not cruelty; it is the mercy of an honest contract, and it is what makes the blessing of Abraham, coming through faith and not through the works of the law, land on a man as sheer gift rather than as wages he had reason to expect.
roots_summary: Hebrew qelalah (H7045), a curse or execration; arar (H779), to curse; berakah (H1293), blessing; Greek katara (G2671), a curse.
roots_lines: Hebrew qelalah (H7045) — a curse, from a root meaning to make light or of no account; the formal covenant sanction.
Hebrew arar (H779) — to curse; the verb repeated twelve times by the Levites in Deuteronomy 27.
Hebrew berakah (H1293) — blessing; the Gerizim half of the pair, never read apart from its counterpart.
Greek katara (G2671) — a curse; Paul's word in Galatians 3, both for what the law brings and for what Christ became.
Greek epikataratos (G1944) — accursed; quoted from the Septuagint of Deuteronomy 21:23, cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.
usage: “he read all the words of the law, the blessings and cursings” — the whole contract, read aloud.
“And all the people shall say, Amen” — Israel consenting to its own sanction.
“our God turned the curse into a blessing” — Balaam at Beth-peor, and the gospel in miniature.

pos: n. pl. (derision endured as persecution; in Hebrews 11:36, the first trial in the list of the unnamed faithful)
etymology: From Old French mocquer, to deride. In Hebrews 11:36 it renders Greek empaigmos, from en and paizo, to play — to make sport of a man, to treat a serious person as an entertainment.
biblical_def:
The eleventh of Hebrews turns at verse 35 from the faith that escaped to the faith that did not, and the catalogue of what the unnamed endured begins with the mouth: And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment. Mockings are named before scourgings, before bonds, before the sawing asunder of the next verse. The Holy Ghost did not rank them by what they do to the body. He ranked them by what they cost a man to bear, and the first thing on the list is being laughed at.

The Greek empaigmos is built on the word for play. To mock a man is to treat him as a diversion — to refuse him the dignity of an argument and hand him to the crowd as sport. That is precisely what was done to Christ: the soldiers bowed the knee, the robe and the reed were props, and the sign over the cross was a joke. Elijah used mockery himself against the prophets of Baal, and the LORD is said to laugh at the wicked, which tells us derision is not in itself sin; it is a weapon, and everything depends on who holds it and against what. What Scripture condemns is the mocking of God's messengers, and 2 Chronicles records the point of no return for Judah in exactly those terms: they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): acts of derision; imitations in contempt; the treating of a person with scorn or ridicule.
webster_full: MOCKING, n. Derision; insult; the act of imitating in contempt.
MOCK, v.t. To imitate in contempt or derision; to mimic for the sake of ridicule; to deride; to laugh at.
DERISION, n. The act of laughing at in contempt; scorn from laughter; contempt manifested by laughter.
SCOURGE, n. A whip; a lash consisting of a strap or cord; hence, a punishment; vindictive affliction.
SCORN, n. Extreme contempt; that disdain which springs from a person's opinion of the meanness of an object.
scriptures: Hebrews 11:36
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment:
Hebrews 11:37
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
2 Chronicles 36:16
But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy.
Jude 1:18
How that they told you there should be mockers in the last time, who should walk after their own ungodly lusts.
corruption_summary: Ridicule now does the work argument used to do, and a generation trained to fear looking foolish more than being wrong is exactly the generation Hebrews 11:36 was written for.
corruption_paragraphs: Mockery is the cheapest instrument of unbelief and the most effective, because it never has to engage. A position that is laughed at does not need to be refuted; it only needs to be made unfashionable, and the young are more afraid of being ridiculous than of being mistaken. This is why Hebrews puts mockings at the head of the list. A man may steel himself for a scourging and find he has no defence against a room that finds him funny. Jude says plainly that mockers belong to the last time and walk after their own ungodly lusts — which locates the derision where it comes from, not in superior insight but in appetite defending itself.

There is a corresponding temptation for those on the receiving end: to answer mockery with mockery and call it boldness. Elijah's sarcasm on Carmel and Paul's sharp irony to the Corinthians show that ridicule is not forbidden outright to a believer; but both were aimed at idols and at pretension, never at the weak, and neither man was defending his own dignity. The principle to recover is the one Hebrews supplies in the surrounding verses: these all obtained a good report through faith, they endured as seeing him who is invisible, and God is not ashamed to be called their God. A man who has that verdict in hand can afford to be laughed at.
roots_summary: Greek empaigmos (G1701), mockery, from paizo, to play; empaiktes (G1703), a mocker; Hebrew laag (H3932), to deride.
roots_lines: Greek empaigmos (G1701) — mockery, the making of sport; used once, at the head of the trials of Hebrews 11:36.
Greek empaiktes (G1703) — a mocker, a scoffer; the men Jude and Peter both say will come in the last time.
Hebrew laag (H3932) — to deride, to stammer at in contempt; used of the nations against Zion.
Hebrew taluim / taalul — mockery, caprice; the sport made of Judah's prophets before the exile.
Greek oneidismos (G3680) — reproach; the reproach of Christ which Moses esteemed greater riches than the treasures in Egypt.
usage: “others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings” — derision listed before the whip.
“they mocked the messengers of God... till there was no remedy” — the point of no return.
“there should be mockers in the last time” — Jude locates the appetite behind the laughter.
